idiom_name: GRDB Database.changesCount after a version-predicated UPDATE (Core Data: app-owned version attribute)
implementation_notes: Neither Core Data nor Vapor Fluent ships a row-version check, so the token is written by hand: keep a version column, run the version-predicated UPDATE through GRDB, and test Database.changesCount (the number of rows modified by the most recent INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) - zero means the copy was stale, which the app then resolves by re-reading and merging. With Core Data the persistence layer tracks objects rather than rows and merges by default, so an explicit version attribute plus save-error handling is the only place a stale edit can be caught; Fluent leaves the same responsibility with the application. For in-memory state, swift-atomics' ManagedAtomic.compareExchange gives the identical contract on an atomic token.
code_sketch:
try dbQueue.write { db in
  try db.execute(sql: """
      UPDATE docs SET body = ?, version = version + 1
      WHERE id = ? AND version = ?
      """, arguments: [body, id, seenVersion])
  if db.changesCount == 0 { throw StaleCopyError() }   // re-read and merge
}
pitfalls: changesCount is per connection and describes the most recent statement; another write (or a trigger) between the UPDATE and the read makes it describe the wrong statement.
Core Data's default merge policies silently keep one side of a conflict, hiding exactly the stale write the token exists to expose.
An NSManagedObjectContext used off its queue can corrupt the version attribute and defeat the comparison.
